text: CH is viewed as a pathway with great potential, particularly because of its more complete hydrocarbon product distribution (including aromatics) and lower H consumption; however, it still needs further scale-up, de- 2 risking, and cost reduction to compete at scale. 2.1.2 Emerging Sustainable/Synthetic Aviation Fuel Production Technologies 2.1.2.1 Methanol-to-Jet MTJ is an emerging SAF pathway currently under review by ASTM with estimated certification by 2026-2027. While technically an “ATJ” pathway, MTJ is chemically distinct from the conventional ATJ process. While ATJ converts C or C alcohols through a multistep 2 4 dehydration–oligomerization–hydrogenation sequence to produce predominantly paraffinic hydrocarbons, MTJ leverages de-risked and industry-vetted petrochemical processes such as methanol-to-olefins or methanol-to-gasoline. These zeolite-based catalytic processes convert methanol into a broad range of hydrocarbons more closely resembling petroleum-derived jet fuel, including not only paraffins, but also isoparaffins, cycloalkanes, and aromatics. However, despite the individual steps being commercialized and TRL 9, no integrated process combining all steps specifically for MTJ has been demonstrated at large scale, contributing to an estimated TRL of 6. One of the principal drivers for MTJ development is the widespread availability of methanol feedstock, with current global production capacity exceeding 100 million metric tons (MMT) annually. For context, if this methanol production were hypothetically redirected entirely towards MTJ, on the order of 35-40 MMT of SAF could be produced annually, representing ~12%–13% of current global jet fuel consumption (Eyberg et al. 2024, IATA 2025d). Similar to ATJ, methanol can be sourced from a wide variety of low-carbon sources, including biomass and waste gasification; industrial off-gases; and e-methanol synthesized from captured CO and 2 renewable hydrogen. This provides a scalable and globally accessible pathway that can integrate or bolt on to existing methanol markets and infrastructure. The ability of MTJ to generate aromatics and higher-density fuel components also offers advantages for meeting aviation fuel specifications, particularly those related to density and seal compatibility, as noted previously. Although the MTJ pathway is not yet ASTM certified, its alignment with mature petrochemical processes and the rapid expansion of global methanol capacity has garnered significant industrial industry—especially across Europe—among key developers like Honeywell/UOP, Topsoe, and Exxon Mobil. 19 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. MTJ has not yet seen significant commercialization due to several technical, economic, and regulatory factors. First, the pathway is not currently certified under ASTM D7566, which as described above can be a lengthy multiyear process. Further, from an economics perspective, MTJ involves multiple catalytic conversion stages and hydrogen-intensive upgrading, making capital and operating costs relatively high, especially when using sources of renewable methanol as a feedstock, which can be multiple orders of magnitude more expensive than conventional fossil-based methanol. Additionally, because the distribution of hydrocarbons produced via MTJ is diverse, spanning light ends (C -C ) to a heavier diesel cut (C ), it requires downstream 1 4 17+ separation and upgrading to meet jet fuel specifications.
